analysis.one_liner: Moves large interstate class-action lawsuits from state courts to federal courts and adds new settlement protections for class members.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in 2003, but it never received a Senate vote before that Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would move most large class-action lawsuits — cases where many people combine similar claims against a company — out of state courts and into federal courts whenever the case exceeds $5 million and involves people from more than one state. It also adds a 'bill of rights' for class members: judges must scrutinize settlements that pay people in coupons instead of cash, settlements must be explained in plain language including what lawyers will be paid, and settlement papers must be sent to state and federal regulators. The federal-court shift was the longtime goal of business groups, who argue state courts favor out-of-state defendants; consumer and trial-lawyer groups say federal courts make it much harder to bring these cases at all.
analysis.who_benefits: Large companies that are frequent class-action defendants — insurers, banks, manufacturers, and consumer-facing corporations — gain the most, because federal courts are widely viewed as less likely to certify classes and to award large judgments than many state courts. Class members also gain modestly from new rules against coupon-only settlements and for clearer settlement notices.

how_it_helps.text: Judges could not approve settlements in which class members get coupons or noncash benefits, or end up paying the lawyers out of their own recovery, without a hearing finding the settlement fair, reasonable, and adequate [S3][S4].
Settlement notices must include a short, plain-language summary covering class members' rights, what defendants must do, and the dollar amount of attorney fees being sought [S3][S4].

Every proposed settlement must be served on the chief regulators in each state where class members live and on federal regulators, and final approval must wait at least 90 days after those officials are notified [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and workers with small-dollar claims bear the cost if the bill passes: their cases would shift to federal court, where class certification standards make it harder to combine many small claims into one suit, so fewer corporate-wrongdoing cases would be brought and settled at all. Plaintiffs' law firms that handle class actions also lose business.

drawbacks.text: Moving cases to federal court makes it harder to certify a class, which means many legitimate claims too small to sue over individually would simply never be brought — the practical effect is less recovery for consumers, not more [S4].

The bill lets any single defendant move a state-court class action to federal court without the consent of the other parties, and lets review of decisions sending cases back to state court be appealed, giving defendants repeated chances to keep cases in federal court [S3].

The state courts that Congress finds biased against out-of-state defendants are often the courts most accessible to ordinary consumers, so the bill's remedy for perceived bias comes at those consumers' expense [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The settlement protections against coupon abuses and for clearer notices are real consumer benefits. But they are secondary to the bill's central effect: shifting interstate class actions to federal court, which corporate defendants have long sought because it is harder to sue them there. For the many consumers whose class claims become too difficult to pursue, the bill trades away the main practical tool for holding companies accountable in exchange for tidier settlement paperwork.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it with amendments and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of business in June 2003, but supporters never got it to the floor for a vote before that Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Grassley introduced the bill on February 4, 2003 with 19 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee [S6][S5].
The committee ordered it reported favorably with amendments on April 11, 2003, and it was reported and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar on June 2, 2003 [S6].
The committee's written report, filed July 31, 2003, included minority views — the committee's Democratic members filed a dissenting statement [S6].
No further action was taken on the bill in the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that are frequent class-action defendants and the state-court system's existing plaintiffs' bar both keep the status quo: the cases that would have moved to federal court stay where they are.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate defendants and state-court plaintiffs' lawyers

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for federal-court jurisdiction over interstate class actions, their top tort-reform priority of the era.

against.what_they_did: Kept the bill from reaching the Senate floor for a vote during the 108th Congress.

against.name: Trial lawyers and consumer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would strip consumers of access to state courts.

sides.party_line_note: Republican senators dominated the bill's support — 19 of its 22 cosponsors were Republicans — while the committee's Democratic minority filed dissenting views, and the bill died without a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would move most large interstate class actions to federal court, where class certification is harder, sharply reducing companies' exposure to state-court class litigation. Their gain comes directly from consumers' reduced ability to band together and sue.
Class actions against large defendants would shift to federal courts that certify fewer classes, shrinking the case supply for plaintiffs' firms. Their fortunes track consumers' ability to recover.
The bill gives special settlement-notification treatment to banks and their regulators, and as frequent class-action defendants they benefit from the federal-court shift.
